question_text: Explain the difference between optimistic and pessimistic concurrency control.
reference_answer: Pessimistic concurrency control locks data when a transaction reads it, preventing conflicts but reducing throughput and risking deadlocks. Optimistic control allows reads without locks and validates a version number or timestamp at commit, rolling back on conflict. Optimistic suits low-contention workloads; pessimistic suits high-contention ones.

question_text: Explain the difference between a process and a thread.
reference_answer: A process is a running program with its own address space and resources. A thread is a lightweight unit of execution inside a process; threads share the process memory, so switching and communication are cheaper but need synchronisation to avoid race conditions.

question_text: What is a database index and how does it affect read and write performance?
expected_structure: Definition -> benefit -> cost -> when to use
reference_answer: An index is a data structure, such as a B-tree, that lets the database locate rows without scanning the whole table, which speeds up reads. Every insert, update or delete must also maintain the index, so writes slow down and storage grows. Index columns used often in filters and joins.

question_text: What is normalization in databases and why is it used?
expected_structure: Definition -> normal forms -> benefits and trade-off
reference_answer: Normalization organises data into related tables to reduce redundancy and update, insert and delete anomalies, following normal forms such as 1NF, 2NF and 3NF. It improves consistency, but more joins can slow some queries, so some systems denormalise selectively.
